raw_graphql_pull_request.body: - [x] I, the PR author, have personally reviewed every line of this PR. # What does this PR do? Adds an opt-in `--inference-gc-mode` (`InferenceConfig.gc_mode`) so that Python's cyclic garbage collector stops stalling dynamic-inference serving: `freeze` keeps long-lived engine state out of every collection, and `freeze_overlap` also runs collections right after a forward pass is queued, so they overlap GPU work. The default mode leaves current behavior unchanged. ## Details ### Problem After startup, an inference process holds millions of GC-tracked objects (model modules, CUDA graph state, compile caches). A CPython full (generation-2) collection scans all of them. On a 4-GPU MoE deployment (TP1, EP4, local CUDA graphs, async scheduling), full collections took 0.65–1.2 s per rank. Each rank collects at a different time, and with expert parallelism the other ranks wait for it. In one trace, a 631 ms collection on one rank left its GPU idle while the other three waited in a barrier kernel. After the CPU submits a decode step, only ~5.6 ms of GPU work remains queued, so moving the collection alone cannot hide it. The collection itself has to get cheaper. ### Change The core logic is in `megatron/core/inference/engines/dynamic_engine.py` - **`freeze`**: after engine setup and after `resume()`, collect, then `gc.freeze()` so that long-lived objects are never scanned again, then collect once more. The second collection resets CPython's record of the old-generation size; without it the next full collection is deferred into one large scan. The engine freezes once more the first time it drains, which covers state built by the first requests (for example kernels compiled on first use). Automatic GC stays on, and its collections now scan only objects created since the freeze. - **`freeze_overlap`**: everything `freeze` does, plus automatic GC is disabled while serving. After each forward pass is queued, `_trigger_gc_now()` runs whichever collection CPython's own thresholds say is due, so it overlaps queued GPU work instead of starting right before the next launch. Idle coordinator ticks (all EP ranks idle) run it too. - **Interface**: `--inference-gc-mode {default,freeze,freeze_overlap}` maps through `InferenceSetupConfig` to `InferenceConfig.gc_mode`. Screenshots below demonstrate the "overlap" effect. Before: gc before graph launch is exposed After: gc overlaps with GPU work Screenshots below demonstrate the "freeze" effect. Before: 1000ms+ gen2 gc After: 13ms gen2 gc ### Safety - Freezing never frees an object early. Reference counting is unaffected. - The cost is that an object alive at a freeze point that later becomes cyclic garbage is kept until `suspend()`. Freezes happen when no requests are in flight to reduce long-lived engine state objects. A unit test checks that a CUDA tensor in a frozen reference cycle is released by `suspend()`, this ensures that we do not cause dead GPU memory blocks. ### Results 4× GB300, TP1/EP4 MoE NT4, 64 requests of 128 tokens per process. `default` (current behavior) was measured in four processes, two of them on a build without this change; each other mode in two. Will attach screenshot to show the effect of freezing. ### Testing - New: `test_gc_mode_releases_frozen_garbage_on_suspend` (`freeze`, `freeze_overlap`) in `test_dynamic_engine.py`, `test_trigger_gc_now_follows_cpython_thresholds` in `test_text_generation_controller.py`, and config and flag tests in `test_inference_config.py`. - Existing engine, async-scheduling, controller and coordinator tests updated where they build engines or controllers without `__init__`. ## Code provenance No code was copied or adapted from external sources. ## Contribution process ### Pre-checks - [x] I have added relevant unit tests - [x] I have added relevant functional tests - [x] If this PR adds or changes a GPU kernel (Triton, `jit_fuser`/`torch.compile`, CUDA extension, TE or external-library dispatch, or a scatter/index accumulation), I have added or updated its bit-exact determinism test and registered it in `tests/unit_tests/determinism/kernels/manifest.py` ([guide](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/blob/main/docs/developer/determinism/testing.md)) - [x] I have added proper typing to my code [Typing guidelines](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html) - [x] I have added relevant documentation - [x] I have run the [autoformatter.sh](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/blob/main/tools/autoformat.sh) on my PR ### Code review Feel free to message or comment `@NVIDIA/mcore-oncall` to help accelerate your merge into main. The less complex your PR is, the faster it will be approved and merged! All PRs start as **draft**. If you open a non-draft PR, it will be automatically converted to draft. #### Step 1: Mark PR as "Ready for Review" 1. When your PR is ready, click **Ready for Review**. 2. An oncall reviewer is auto-assigned and expert reviewers are notified based on your changes. - Some PRs may jump straight to step 2. This is determined by `.github/CODEOWNERS`. :warning: Only mark as ready once merge-conflicts are resolved and the CI is passing. Final Review might get declined if these requirements are not fulfilled. #### Step 2: Final Review For PRs that change `megatron/core`, once all expert reviewers have approved, the `Final Review` label is applied **automatically** and final reviewers are assigned. For PRs outside `megatron/core`, this step is skipped. #### Step 3: Approved Once all required reviewers have approved, the `Approved` label is applied **automatically**. ### Merge Any member of [mcore-engineers](https://github.com/orgs/NVIDIA/teams/mcore-engineers) will be able to merge your PR.

Auto-sync is disabled for draft pull requests in this repository. Workflows must be run manually.

Contributors can view more details about this message [here](https://docs.gha-runners.nvidia.com/cpr/auto-sync).

This pull request requires additional validation before any workflows can run on NVIDIA's runners.

Pull request vetters can view their responsibilities [here](https://docs.gha-runners.nvidia.com/cpr/vetters).

Contributors can view more details about this message [here](https://docs.gha-runners.nvidia.com/cpr/contributors).

Thanks for looking into this! 

I'm on the fence about whether we should turn this on by default, since it is quite useful when encountered but difficult to reliably trigger. I know other frameworks have it as opt-in. We're trying to make all new optimizations default-on when it makes sense to avoid performance benchmarks missing important flags which they didn't know about and are rare/not well-known. Is there a reason you see to *not* turn this on by default?

On torch >= 2.9 this fallback shouldn't run at all. `cuda_graphs.py` only freezes and unfreezes around a capture when FREEZE_GC is true, and it forces that to False on torch >= 2.9, so an inline capture doesn't touch the frozen heap. Switching overlap off and scheduling a refreeze unnecessarily costs real performance, because overlap stays off until the next full drain, which may never come under sustained load. Can we gate on FREEZE_GC additionally?

I do recognize that the real problem here is that we should get rid of the pre-torch 2.9 path. Unfortunately it looks like the repo will support torch < 2.9 for a little longer.

> I'm on the fence about whether we should turn this on by default

I think it should be on by default, not enabling it by default is just following existing codebase convention. If team is moving towards enabling optimizations by default, would love to do that!

For the monkey-patching in `dynamic_engine.py` for the inline capture corner case, should I just remove it if it is not on a hot production path? In the worst case, that I remove my patch, and the inline capture is triggered, the code just runs less efficiently due to GC being unfrozen, but should not break.

     """Mode used to schedule dynamic batching inference work. Defaults to async scheduling; use
     ``AsyncScheduleMode.LEGACY`` to disable it."""
 
+    gc_mode: Literal["default", "freeze", "freeze_overlap"] = "freeze_overlap"
+    """Python garbage collection policy while the engine serves requests.

+    def _enter_custom_gc_mode(self) -> None:
+        """Apply `gc_mode` after CUDA graph capture during engine start or resume.
+
+        `cuda_graphs.py` brackets each capture with a process-wide `gc.freeze()` and
+        `gc.unfreeze()`, so a graph captured inline later, for a batch shape that
+        `create_cuda_graphs` skipped, would unfreeze the heap frozen here. Serving is not
+        expected to hit that path.
+        """
+        if self.gc_mode == "default":
+            return
+        self._in_custom_gc_mode = True
+        self._collect_and_freeze_gc()
+        # freeze_pending=True means we want to freeze again when the engine first drains,
+        # after the first requests have built their long-lived state. A drain only counts
+        # after an engine step has run, so we need to record the _gc_mode_entry_step.
+        self._gc_freeze_pending = True
+        self._gc_mode_entry_step = self.context.step_count
+
+    def _freeze_gc_after_first_request_drain(self) -> None:
+        """Freeze the state built by the first requests, then start scheduled collection."""
+        self._gc_freeze_pending = False
+        self._collect_and_freeze_gc()
+        if self.gc_mode == "freeze_overlap":
+            # Automatic GC stays on until here. Disabling it from engine setup left all garbage
+            # from first-use kernel compilation for one long collection after the first forward.
+            self._gc_was_enabled = gc.isenabled()
+            gc.disable()
+            self.controller._overlap_gc = True
+
+    def _collect_and_freeze_gc(self) -> None:
+        """Collect, then exclude long-lived engine objects from later GC scans."""
+        gc.collect()
+        gc.freeze()
+        # A second collect() is needed for freeze() to take effect.
+        gc.collect()
+
+    def _collect_gc_while_idle(self, drained: bool) -> None:
+        """Do the GC work `gc_mode` owes while every EP rank is idle."""
+        if not self._in_custom_gc_mode:
+            return
+        if self._gc_freeze_pending:
+            if drained and self.context.step_count > self._gc_mode_entry_step:
+                self._freeze_gc_after_first_request_drain()
+        elif self.controller._overlap_gc:
+            self.controller._trigger_gc_now()
+
+    def _exit_custom_gc_mode(self) -> None:
+        """Stop using custom `gc_mode` and go back to the Python default GC mode."""
+        if not self._in_custom_gc_mode:
+            return
+        self._in_custom_gc_mode = False
+        self._gc_freeze_pending = False
+        if self.controller._overlap_gc:
+            self.controller._overlap_gc = False
+            if self._gc_was_enabled:
+                gc.enable()
+        gc.collect()
+        gc.unfreeze()
+        # Anything collected now became cyclic garbage while frozen, so freezing kept it alive.
+        allocated = torch.cuda.memory_allocated()
+        collected = gc.collect()
+        if collected:
+            logger.info(
+                f"gc_mode={self.gc_mode} retained {collected} garbage objects holding "
+                f"{allocated - torch.cuda.memory_allocated()} bytes of CUDA memory until now"
+            )

+        """Frozen cyclic garbage, including its CUDA memory, is released by suspend.
+
+        Scheduled collection starts only when the engine first drains after setup or resume.
+        """
+        was_enabled = gc.isenabled()
+        overlap = gc_mode == "freeze_overlap"
+        # Collections move immortal objects into the generation that gc.freeze() uses.
+        gc.unfreeze()
+        gc.collect()
+        immortal_count = gc.get_freeze_count()
+        try:
+            env = self._build_test_env(DynamicEngineTestConfig(gc_mode=gc_mode))
+            engine = env.engine
+            assert gc.get_freeze_count() > immortal_count
+            assert engine._gc_freeze_pending
+            assert not engine.controller._overlap_gc
+            assert gc.isenabled() is was_enabled
+
+            # A CUDA tensor in a reference cycle that is alive when the heap is frozen.
+            cycle = [torch.ones(1 << 20, device="cuda")]
+            cycle_bytes = cycle[0].untyped_storage().nbytes()
+            cycle_tensor = weakref.ref(cycle[0])
+            cycle.append(cycle)
+            engine._collect_and_freeze_gc()
+            del cycle
+            gc.collect()
+            assert cycle_tensor() is not None
+
+            half = len(env.requests) // 2

+            assert not engine._gc_freeze_pending

+            engine.suspend()
+            # Earlier engines kept alive by pending event-loop callbacks may be released too.

inline_comments.body:
On torch >= 2.9 this fallback shouldn't run at all. `cuda_graphs.py` only freezes and unfreezes around a capture when FREEZE_GC is true, and it forces that to False on torch >= 2.9, so an inline capture doesn't touch the frozen heap. Switching overlap off and scheduling a refreeze unnecessarily costs real performance, because overlap stays off until the next full drain, which may never come under sustained load. Can we gate on FREEZE_GC additionally?

I do recognize that the real problem here is that we should get rid of the pre-torch 2.9 path. Unfortunately it looks like the repo will support torch < 2.9 for a little longer.

> I'm on the fence about whether we should turn this on by default

I think it should be on by default, not enabling it by default is just following existing codebase convention. If team is moving towards enabling optimizations by default, would love to do that!

For the monkey-patching in `dynamic_engine.py` for the inline capture corner case, should I just remove it if it is not on a hot production path? In the worst case, that I remove my patch, and the inline capture is triggered, the code just runs less efficiently due to GC being unfrozen, but should not break.

reviews.body:
Thanks for looking into this! 

I'm on the fence about whether we should turn this on by default, since it is quite useful when encountered but difficult to reliably trigger. I know other frameworks have it as opt-in. We're trying to make all new optimizations default-on when it makes sense to avoid performance benchmarks missing important flags which they didn't know about and are rare/not well-known. Is there a reason you see to *not* turn this on by default?
